# New opportunities at the wild frontier

## Authors

- Jane Alfred<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-6798-0064](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6798-0064)) †
- Ian T Baldwin<sup>2</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-5371-2974](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5371-2974)) †

### Affiliations

1. Cambridge United Kingdom
2. Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology Jena Germany

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

A better understanding of the natural history of model organisms will increase their value as model systems and also keep them at the forefront of research.

## Introduction

Many of the fundamental principles of biology were discovered by developing a model organism to investigate a biological question. The principles of heredity, the genetic code, transcription, translation and DNA replication were a few of the landmark discoveries made in Drosophila melanogaster, the rock-star model insect, and Escherichia coli, the model bacterium. But how representative are these models of the ‘rest of life’, as is often assumed? And how do the laboratory lives of model organisms compare with those of their relatives in the wild and those of other closely related species? Surprisingly, we know very little about the real lives of many model organisms, but it is clear that some of them are not very representative of their species.

To explore these questions further, eLife has invited a number of researchers to write about the natural histories of some of the best-established model organisms used in biological research, among them the zebrafish Danio rerio; the plants, maize and Arabidopsis thaliana; the nematode, Caenorhabitis elegans; and the microorganisms, Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These articles, together with future additions to this series, consider how a better understanding of the natural history of model organisms can extend and enhance their value as model organisms and also keep them at the forefront of cutting edge biological research (http://elifesciences.org/natural-history-of-model-organisms).

By providing a natural history context to these much loved, but decontextualized, research organisms, we hope that the articles in this series will help to heal the unhappy division of biology departments along cellular-molecular-developmental and ecological-evolutionary lines. This split, which is reflected in many graduate training programmes, is largely responsible for the dearth of natural history information about these model organisms. We also hope that these articles will prepare a more unified family of biologists to anticipate the research possibilities of a not-too-distant future, when the distinctions between model and non-model organisms become blurred.

## Supermodels are not always representative

Just as the supermodels of the fashion world do not represent the average Homo sapiens, some ‘supermodel organisms’ do not represent their nearest relatives or even their own species. Moreover, some of these supermodel organisms have never lived in the wild. The crop plant maize is one such example, and the conversion of the wild grass teosinte into maize some 7–10,000 years ago is perhaps the first example of biotechnological innovation by humans. The domestication of the yeast S. cerevisiae for brewing and baking happened around the same period. House mice and the nematode, C. elegans, also share a long evolutionary history with humans, becoming human commensals when our houses and orchards became their habitats, but they do not owe their existence to humans. The relationship of other model organisms with humans is more recent. For example, humans distribute the marine model organism Ciona intestinalis—an organism that is of increasing interest to evolutionary biologists because it occupies a key branch point in the evolution of chordates—around the world's oceans via ships.

In many cases, model organisms differ from their closest non-model relatives by possessing particular traits that have facilitated their domestication and adaptation to the laboratory environment, and over time this process has accentuated the differences between model organisms and their wild relatives. However, some model organisms, such as C. intestinalis, have not (as yet) been adapted to breed in the laboratory. While this raises certain challenges (data generated from locally collected specimens, for example, might differ significantly from that stored in community databases), it also offers opportunities to study important evolutionary processes, such as adaptation and variation.

![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/06956/elife-06956-fig1-v1.jpg)

As these articles highlight, many model organisms have a boom-and-bust lifestyle: C. elegans and D. melanogaster, for example, both colonize rotting food sources in the wild, reproducing rapidly when food is available. As a result, they have rapid life cycles while food is abundant, making generation times short, which is an ideal attribute for studying heritable traits and for generating experimental populations. In the wild, A. thaliana is highly successful at reproducing rapidly in poor habitats when environmental conditions are good. Its resulting short generation time, combined with its ability to self fertilize and its small condensed genome, make it an ideal plant for research purposes.

But selecting for these highly-favoured, rapid-cycling traits has consequences. It means that some of our favourite models tend to be ‘ecological escape artists’ that avoid rather confront the selection pressures imposed by predators, the environment and competitors—pressures that longer-lived, slower-growing species must cope with through adaptation. Unfortunately, the ability of some model organisms to escape selection pressures has severely limited the traits that can be studied in these systems, meaning that ecologists and evolutionary biologists are often not able to study the traits they are most interested in. Arabidopsis, for example has a wonderfully simple root system, which is ideal for imaging developmental processes, but it lacks the structural complexity that is likely to be important for plants with non-ruderal lifestyles. Moreover, Arabidopsis does not have any associations with mycorrhizal fungi, a symbiotic association of great importance for most land plants, and of significant agricultural importance too. And as a successful self fertilizer, its flowers are also of little interest to pollinators and, consequently, to the biologists who investigate them.

## Genomics to the rescue

With the availability of inexpensive short-read sequencing methods, literally hundreds of strains of many supermodel organisms have been sequenced and assembled, providing population biologists with the data they require to conduct ‘reverse ecology’ (Li et al., 2008). This approach uncovers genomic imprints left by past selection pressures, offering insights into trait evolution in the course of an organism's natural history. It also affords new opportunities to test directly associations between genotype and phenotype. But researchers still need to discover and collect the most informative strains to sequence, and this requires good old-fashioned field work.

The authors of the articles in this series represent a growing generation of systems biologists who are seeking out the still-feral relatives of our laboratory models. Their articles highlight that much remains to be learnt about the basic ecology of these model organisms and they provide a tantalizing view of the new frontiers that remain to be explored when we place these well-investigated organisms, and our knowledge of their biology, into a natural history context.

For example, S. cerevisiae has been found in the bark of oak trees and in primary forests in China that are remote from human activity. Perhaps it is only a coincidence that wine makers have favoured oak as a material for constructing wine barrels and casks. More interestingly, S. cerevisiae has also been found in the faecal human microbiome in particular populations, suggesting a much more intimate association with humans than had been previously suspected.

Knowing the natural habitats of model organisms is essential for understanding key aspects of their biology. Habitats can shape behaviours, such as foraging and shoaling, and can inform our understanding of life cycles and predator-prey relationships, as well as an organism's ability to adapt to different environmental conditions. By understanding habitat and lifestyle we can also gain insights into the processes that shape the genomes of the organisms used in research, a key feature of their biology. The sampling of wild populations of zebrafish has revealed, for example, that they contain extensive levels of genetic diversity, only a fraction of which is seen in lab strains of these fish.

## In the future everyone can be a model

Recent advances in high-throughput, genome-wide approaches and in genome-editing technologies, such as CRISPR/CAS9, allow the genomes of non-model and wild organisms to be manipulated (Chen et al., 2014; Doudna and Charpentier, 2014). As such, the particular traits that made our model organisms easy to domesticate need no longer limit the scope of scientific inquiry. The consequent blurring of the model/non-model boundary could, in the future, bring together currently disparate biological faculties, uniting them in their search to understand the important traits that are distributed throughout all biodiversity.

Our planet's biological legacy lies in the astounding array of solutions that evolutionary processes have found for all of the challenges that organisms face in all habitats on this planet. In the not-too-distant future, we will need to harvest food and other resources from most habitats on earth and to produce substantially more efficient crops to sustain our burgeoning human population (Ronald, 2014). And this will require a deeper understanding of the genetic traits that have made some organisms particularly efficient, stress-tolerant and clever at solving ecological challenges. Achieving this aim will require us to develop a unified approach to biology, one that marries the skills of ecologists and organismal biologists with those of molecular biologists. We hope that the articles in this series will help to bring these potential partners together.

claims.claim: Maize has never lived in the wild.
claims.source: Moreover, some of these supermodel organisms have never lived in the wild. The crop plant maize is one such example, and the conversion of the wild grass teosinte into maize some 7–10,000 years ago is perhaps the first example of biotechnological innovation by humans.
claims.evidence: This draws from established scientific consensus about maize domestication.

claims.claim: Many model organisms have a boom-and-bust lifestyle.
claims.source: As these articles highlight, many model organisms have a boom-and-bust lifestyle: C. elegans and D. melanogaster, for example, both colonize rotting food sources in the wild, reproducing rapidly when food is available.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to articles in the series being discussed.

results.result: The authors argue that there is a dearth of natural history information about model organisms, which they attribute to the split of biology departments along cellular-molecular-developmental and ecological-evolutionary lines. This split is reflected in graduate training programs and has resulted in limited knowledge about the real lives of many model organisms, some of which are not representative of their species.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 are inferences about the state of knowledge in the field without quantitative support. Claims C16 and C17 propose a causal relationship between departmental structure and knowledge gaps, but this is presented as inference rather than demonstrated empirically. No data is provided to substantiate the extent of the knowledge gap or the causal mechanism.

results.result: The authors claim that fundamental principles of biology including heredity, the genetic code, transcription, translation, and DNA replication were discovered using Drosophila melanogaster and Escherichia coli as model organisms.
results.evaluation: While these organisms contributed significantly to molecular biology, the claims oversimplify the historical record. For example, the genetic code was primarily elucidated using cell-free systems and various organisms, not exclusively D. melanogaster and E. coli. The principles of heredity were established by Mendel using peas, and later extended by Morgan using Drosophila. This represents a misattribution of discoveries to specific model organisms.

results.result: The authors describe the domestication history of maize and yeast, stating that maize was converted from teosinte 7-10,000 years ago and has never lived in the wild, while S. cerevisiae was domesticated for brewing and baking around the same period. They suggest maize domestication may be the first example of biotechnological innovation by humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C20, and C85 are well-established in the scientific literature regarding the timing and nature of maize and yeast domestication. Claim C19 is appropriately hedged with 'perhaps,' acknowledging the speculative nature of claiming this as the 'first' biotechnological innovation, as other domestication events occurred around the same time period.

results.result: The authors argue that model organisms differ from their wild relatives due to traits facilitating laboratory domestication, and that this process has accentuated differences over time. They note that some organisms like C. intestinalis have not been adapted to laboratory breeding, which presents both challenges and opportunities.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C28 are well-supported inferences based on established principles of artificial selection and domestication. Claim C29 is factual knowledge about C. intestinalis breeding status. Claim C30 appropriately presents data variability as a speculation ('might differ') rather than a certainty, acknowledging the uncertainty inherent in this situation.

results.result: The authors describe the boom-and-bust lifestyle of model organisms like C. elegans, D. melanogaster, and A. thaliana, which colonize ephemeral food sources and reproduce rapidly when resources are available. This results in short generation times that make these organisms ideal for studying heritable traits and generating experimental populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C86 are supported by citations to articles in the series. Claims C35-C37 and C39-C42 represent well-established knowledge about these model organisms' biology and their utility for research. The logical connection between life history traits and research utility is sound and well-supported.

results.result: The authors argue that many model organisms are 'ecological escape artists' that avoid selection pressures rather than adapting to them, which has limited the traits that can be studied in these systems and prevented ecologists and evolutionary biologists from studying traits of interest.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C45-C46 present reasonable inferences about the limitations of model organisms for ecological and evolutionary research. Claim C44 represents established knowledge about life history evolution. The argument is logically coherent: organisms selected for rapid reproduction in resource-rich environments lack traits related to coping with predation, competition, and environmental stress.

results.result: The authors provide Arabidopsis as an example of model organism limitations, noting its simple root system is ideal for imaging but lacks complexity important for non-ruderal plants, it lacks mycorrhizal associations important for most land plants and agriculture, and its self-fertilization makes it uninteresting to pollination biologists.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C50-C52 represent well-established knowledge about Arabidopsis biology and mycorrhizal importance. Claims C48, C53-C54 are reasonable inferences about research utility. Claim C49 is appropriately hedged as speculation ('likely to be important'). Together, these claims effectively illustrate the limitations of model organisms for certain research questions.

results.result: The authors describe how inexpensive sequencing has enabled hundreds of strains of model organisms to be sequenced, providing data for 'reverse ecology' approaches that uncover genomic signatures of past selection and enable genotype-phenotype associations. However, this still requires field work to collect informative strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by citation to Li et al., 2008. Claims C57-C58 represent established knowledge about reverse ecology methods. Claims C59-C60 are reasonable inferences about the applications and requirements of this approach. The logic connecting genomic data to ecological insights is sound.

results.result: The authors describe discoveries about S. cerevisiae natural habitats, including oak bark and remote Chinese forests, and its presence in human gut microbiomes. They speculate about potential connections to wine-making practices and suggest a more intimate human association than previously suspected.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 and C65 represent established knowledge about yeast ecology. Claim C63 is factual knowledge about wine-making. Claim C64 is appropriately presented as speculation ('perhaps... only a coincidence'). Claim C66 is a reasonable inference from the microbiome data. The claims effectively illustrate how natural history research reveals unexpected findings about model organisms.

results.result: The authors argue that knowing natural habitats is essential for understanding model organism biology, as habitats shape behaviors, life cycles, predator-prey relationships, and adaptation. Understanding habitat and lifestyle provides insights into genomic evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 represent well-established ecological principles. Claims C67 and C72 are reasonable inferences about the importance of natural history for understanding biology. The argument is logically sound: ecological context is necessary for interpreting organismal traits and genomic features.

results.result: The authors report that wild zebrafish populations contain extensive genetic diversity, with lab strains containing only a fraction of this diversity.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge about zebrafish population genetics and the genetic bottleneck effect of laboratory domestication. This is a well-documented phenomenon across model organisms and illustrates the value of studying wild populations.

results.result: The authors argue that advances in genome-editing technologies like CRISPR/Cas9 allow manipulation of non-model organisms, meaning the traits that made organisms easy to domesticate need no longer limit scientific inquiry. This could blur the model/non-model boundary and unite disparate biological disciplines.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by appropriate citations. Claims C77-C78 are reasonable speculations about future research directions, appropriately hedged with conditional language ('need no longer,' 'could'). The logic is sound: if any organism can be genetically manipulated, the historical advantages of model organisms become less important.

results.result: The authors present the thesis that better understanding of model organism natural history will increase their value and keep them at the forefront of research. They describe an eLife editorial initiative inviting articles about the natural histories of established model organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 are speculative assertions about future benefits that are not empirically demonstrated in this manuscript. Claims C10-C15 are factual statements about the editorial initiative. While the thesis is plausible, no evidence is provided to support that natural history knowledge actually increases model organism value or research prominence.

results.result: The authors describe the evolutionary relationships between humans and various model organisms, including house mice and C. elegans as commensals that don't owe their existence to humans, and C. intestinalis as a marine organism distributed by ships that is of interest for chordate evolution studies.
results.evaluation: All claims represent well-established knowledge about the ecology, evolution, and phylogenetic importance of these organisms. The distinction between commensalism and domestication is accurately presented, and the description of C. intestinalis dispersal and evolutionary significance is correct.

results.result: The authors argue that future food security will require harvesting resources from diverse habitats and producing more efficient crops, necessitating deeper understanding of genetic traits conferring efficiency and stress tolerance. This will require a unified biological approach integrating ecology, organismal biology, and molecular biology.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 represents established knowledge about evolution and biodiversity. Claims C80-C82 are speculations about future needs, with C80-C81 supported by citation to Ronald 2014. Claims C83-C84 are speculative assertions about required organizational changes in biology. While the arguments are plausible, they represent opinion about future directions rather than demonstrated results.
